title: Trying to get AI to invent a game like Go. But what even makes a game like Go good?
author: rbrthogan1
selftext:
I wrote up this fun side project on getting AI models to generate good 2 player perfect information board game ideas and then testing their quality via self-play.

Would love to hear what game players think of how I measured it

comments.author: Skubcraft
comments.body: Its simplicity and how that lends to deep complexity. Learn in 10 minutes, take a lifetime to master.

replies.author: rbrthogan1
replies.body: Exactly! I tried to make this quantifiable and then used that metric as test for AI generated games. Spoiler: long way to go

comments.author: gay_married
comments.body:
The main things that make Go work are:

1. High branching factor. There are many valid moves.

2. Universal rules. No matter where you place a stone, it follows the same rules

3. Good reaaons to place a stone in many different places. There are advantages to shoring up your position, extending, attacking, or claiming green territory. These goals are all in tension. 

4. Inevitability. The game ends. It is much harder to remove stones than to add them, and once they're removed, there usually isn't a reason to keep playing there (except snapbacks)

replies.author: rbrthogan1
replies.body: Nice list. I think my framework in the post manages to capture most of this mathematically? Do you agree? The goal is to find a way to objectively measure a list like yours and apply to other games (human or AI generated)

replies.author: rbrthogan1
replies.body:
I would say that Hassabis's standard for "creative invention" is probably not well enough defined. I think that the overwhelming majority of human creativity comes from connecting different parts of human culture, or by minimal extension of it. I think models can certainly do that but I think we are still very early in understanding how to make them do it well. My IdeaEvolve project is one attempt to improve that.  
  
Something radically and truly new seems harder. But also very hard to think of examples of humans doing it. As a physicist, I reach for Einstein's relativity insight, but I think we probably need more and better examples.  
  
Basically, I think we really don't understand creativity well enough to definitively refute that LLMs can do it.
